intro: This guide leads a group of teenagers, aged about 13 to 18, through “The Pursuit of God (For Teens)” in eleven weeks, one chapter a week. A. W. Tozer, a self-taught Chicago pastor, wrote the book in 1948 for Christians who knew plenty about God but were still hungry for God himself; the teen edition follows his ten chapters in order, adds an opening chapter about his life, and keeps his prayers in his own words. It suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group, especially teens who have grown up in church and want more than the right answers.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or beforehand at home. Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you lead. Do the activity, which takes about ten minutes. Close by praying Tozer’s prayer from the chapter, or your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and pray Tozer’s prayer before you lead it; his prayers are honest, and teens notice when a leader means them. Week 3 retells Abraham being asked to offer Isaac, which can disturb some readers, so read it calmly and stress what the chapter stresses: God stopped him and Isaac went home alive. Several chapters ask teens to name what they cling to or the ‘self-sins’ in them; keep all of that private and never ask anyone to read out what they wrote. The book is frank that Tozer’s devotion made him distant from his wife and children, and that he spoke sharply about other churches; treat both honestly and gently, as the teen edition does. A few weeks need nothing; most need only paper and pens.

weeks.summary: We meet A. W. Tozer, who had no high school or seminary education, gave his life to Christ in an attic at about seventeen, and pastored in Chicago for thirty-one years, often praying face-down on his study floor; the chapter is also honest that this absorption made him distant from his wife and seven children. In his preface Tozer grieves to see “God’s children starving while actually seated at the Father’s table,” insists that “it is not mere words that nourish the soul, but God Himself,” and calls his own fire “not large” but “real.” The big idea: knowing about God is not the same as knowing God, and hunger for him is a good sign.

memory_verse.text: You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart.

activity.title: Facts or Friendship?
steps: Ask everyone to write down, quickly, three facts they know about a celebrity or sports star, and three facts they know about a close friend.
Discuss: what is the difference between knowing facts about someone and actually knowing them?
Read Tozer’s line, “it is not mere words that nourish the soul, but God Himself,” and ask how this applies to Bible knowledge.

Give everyone a few quiet minutes to finish this sentence privately and honestly: “What I actually want from God is…” Ask them to keep it somewhere safe, because they will look at it again in the last week.

weeks.summary: Tozer says “God is always previous”: we only seek God because he first sought us, yet we must respond, because finding God is the start of a lifelong pursuit, not the end. He warns that Christians can lose God “amid the wonders of His Word,” that Jesus “waits to be wanted,” and that our great woe lies in seeking God “and” something else. His prayer admits his lack of desire: “I want to want Thee.” The big idea: you can start wherever you are, even if all you can honestly say is that you want to want God.

memory_verse.text: My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.

activity.title: God And…
steps: Read Tozer’s line, “In the ‘and’ lies our great woe,” and explain what he means: seeking God plus something else.
As a group, brainstorm the ‘ands’ that teenagers often add: God and grades, God and being liked, God and a future that goes to plan.
Talk about why these things are not bad in themselves, and how you can tell when one has become what you are really chasing.
Ask each person to write privately their own biggest ‘and’, then pray Tozer’s short prayer together: “God, I want to want you.”

weeks.summary: Tozer says things were meant to stay outside our hearts, but sin moved them inside, so that “my” and “mine” rule us and God’s gifts take God’s place. He tells how Abraham was asked to offer Isaac, wrestled through the night, chose to trust God, and was stopped before he harmed the boy: “He had everything, but he possessed nothing.” His prayer admits fear: “I come trembling, but I do come.” The big idea: giving things to God does not mean losing them; it means they no longer hold us.

memory_verse.text: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

activity.title: Open Hands
steps: Ask everyone to clench a fist tightly for thirty seconds, then open their hand palm up. Talk about the difference between gripping something and holding it on an open hand.
Read Tozer’s summary of Abraham: “He had everything, but he possessed nothing.” Ask: what did Abraham lose on the mountain, and what did he keep?
Discuss which kinds of things are hardest for teenagers to hold with an open hand: a friendship, a dream, a reputation, a plan.
Ask each person to write privately, by name, the one thing they would find hardest to hand to God, and to pray over it silently: “I come trembling, but I do come.”

weeks.summary: Tozer walks through the tabernacle to the Holy of Holies, hidden behind a veil that was torn from top to bottom when Jesus died, opening the way to God for everyone. Yet many Christians stay in the outer courts because of another veil inside them, “the self-life,” woven from self-righteousness, self-pity, self-confidence, self-sufficiency, self-admiration and self-love, which can hide comfortably even in church. Only God can tear it, and though “It is never fun to die,” resurrection follows. The big idea: God opened the way from his side; our part is to stop defending the curtain.

memory_verse.text: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. And the earth shook, and the rocks were split.

activity.title: Spot the Self-Word
activity.materials: Slips of paper with short scenarios
steps: Write Tozer’s six self-words where everyone can see them: self-righteousness, self-pity, self-confidence, self-sufficiency, self-admiration, self-love.
Read out a few short made-up scenarios, such as “After a bad match, Sam replays all the ways it wasn’t fair” or “Jess checks how many likes her post got every ten minutes.”
For each scenario, ask the group which self-word fits best, and why it might be hard to notice in yourself.
Ask each person to circle privately the self-word that stings most for them, and to tell God about it each night this week. Nobody shares which one.

weeks.summary: Tozer says that for many people, Christians included, God is “an inference, not a reality,” though the Bible speaks of tasting, hearing and seeing him. He explains that faith is not imagination: “Faith creates nothing; it simply reckons upon that which is already there.” The visible world is “clamorous” and crowds out the spiritual, yet God is here now, waiting for our response. The big idea: God is real and present, and faith means counting on what is already true.

memory_verse.text: Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!

activity.title: What Is Shouting at You?
steps: Ask everyone to list, on their own, all the things that demanded their attention in the last 24 hours: notifications, people, shows, tasks.
Read Tozer’s words that the visible world is “clamorous, insistent and self-demonstrating,” and ask how many items on their lists ‘shouted’.
Discuss Tozer’s difference between imagining God and reckoning on him. Ask: what would it look like to count on God being present in an ordinary moment?
Challenge everyone to take one walk this week with no earbuds, thanking God for real things they can see, hear and feel, and saying quietly, “And you are here too.”

weeks.summary: Tozer says God’s presence simply means “God is here,” everywhere, so that your bedroom is as close to God as a cathedral; Jacob’s problem, and ours, was “Surely the Lord is in this place; and I knew it not.” The difference between people who find God and those who don’t is not with God but with us, in what Tozer calls “spiritual receptivity,” which grows by exercise and dies by neglect. The big idea: we don’t need to travel to God; we need to wake up to him where we are.

memory_verse.text: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?

activity.title: Mapping the Week
steps: Ask each person to draw a simple map or list of the places they will be this week: home, school, bus, training, a friend’s house.
Read Tozer’s line, “No point is nearer to God than any other point,” and ask which of those places feels least ‘spiritual’, and why.
Discuss Tozer’s picture of the father and son who grow nearer while living in the same house. What would growing nearer to God look like in an ordinary week?
Ask everyone to circle three places on their map where they will pause this week and say, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I know it.”

weeks.summary: Tozer says calling Jesus “the Word” shows that God speaks, and not only in the past: “Not God spoke, but God is speaking.” The Bible is alive because God still speaks through it, but we have “trained our ears not to hear,” explaining things away like the crowd who said “It thundered.” He even marks one of his ideas as only his own opinion, and urges us to get still and come to the Bible “expecting it to speak to you.” The big idea: God is still speaking, and we hear him by getting quiet and listening.

memory_verse.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

activity.title: Expecting It to Speak
steps: Ask everyone to put their phones out of reach, then read 1 Samuel 3:1–10 aloud slowly.
Give two minutes of silence. Ask each person to read the passage again on their own and write down one sentence that stands out.
Invite anyone who wishes to share their sentence and why it caught their attention. Nobody has to.
Close by praying together Samuel’s words, “Speak, for your servant hears,” and encourage everyone to try ten phone-free minutes with the Bible this week.

weeks.summary: Tozer turns to the bronze snake in Numbers 21, which Jesus pointed to, and concludes that looking and believing are the same thing: “faith is the gaze of a soul upon a saving God,” a continuous gaze rather than a one-off act. Faith is like an eye that never sees itself, so instead of anxiously checking whether we have enough faith, we look at Jesus, and when our attention wanders we come back like “a wandering bird coming back to its window.” The big idea: faith is not staring at your faith but looking at Jesus.

memory_verse.text: Looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

activity.title: Tuned to One Fork
steps: Read Numbers 21:8–9 and John 3:14–15 aloud, and ask the group what the bitten Israelites had to do to live.
Discuss Tozer’s picture of faith as an eye that sees everything but itself. Ask: why might constantly checking our own faith make things worse?
Explain Tozer’s hundred pianos tuned to one tuning fork. Ask the group what it would mean for your youth group if each person kept looking to Jesus.
Challenge everyone this week to take one breath and turn their attention to Jesus each time they unlock their phone, before opening anything.

weeks.summary: Tozer says our deepest trouble is a “moral dislocation,” being out of place with God, and that the test of who is first is not what we say but what we choose between God and money, people, ambition or comfort. The key is three words from the Psalms, “Be thou exalted,” and Tozer says “Not perfection, but holy intention made the difference” for people like Abraham and David. His prayer offers God every area of life: possessions, friendships, comforts, reputation and ambitions. The big idea: putting God first does not make us smaller; it puts our lives back in place.

memory_verse.text: Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!

activity.title: Over My…
steps: Read Tozer’s long prayer aloud slowly, pausing after each area he names.
Ask everyone to list the areas privately: possessions, friendships, comforts, reputation, ambitions, family.
Ask them to put a mark beside the line they could pray honestly today, and a question mark beside the one they find hardest. These stay private.
Discuss Tozer’s point that God looks at holy intention, not perfection, and encourage everyone to pray one line each morning this week.

weeks.summary: Tozer says the human race looks like the Beatitudes turned inside out: pride, pleasure-seeking and arrogance instead of humility, mourning and meekness. Jesus offers rest from two inner burdens: pride, which smarts at every slight, and pretence, “the fear of being found out.” The meek man is not “a human mouse” but knows he is nothing in himself and everything in God, so he lets God defend him and accepts himself as he is. The big idea: Jesus offers the rest that comes when we stop competing, stop pretending and let him carry the yoke with us.

memory_verse.text: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.

activity.title: Would You Rather
steps: Ask a few “would you rather” questions and let people move to one side of the room or the other: be admired for something you’re not, or overlooked for something you are? Win and look arrogant, or lose and be gracious? Post your best moment, or share an honest one with a close friend?
After each question, ask one or two people from each side to explain their choice.
Read Tozer’s humorous self-talk about being “pretty small stuff,” and discuss how humour and honesty can take the sting out of feeling overlooked.
Challenge everyone to spend one week posting or sending nothing whose main purpose is to make them look better than they are.

weeks.summary: Tozer’s last chapter attacks the split between “sacred” and “secular” life, pointing out that Paul tells us to eat and drink to God’s glory, so every good, ordinary act can be offered to God. “It is not what a man does that determines whether his work is sacred or secular, it is why he does it,” and for such a person “the whole world” becomes “a sanctuary.” The chapter ends honestly: Tozer’s hunger for God made him distant from his family, and his own teaching points the better way. The big idea: done for God, your ordinary Tuesday is as holy as your Sunday.

memory_verse.text: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

activity.title: Sacred or Secular?
activity.materials: Two signs reading “Sacred” and “Secular”, and slips of paper
steps: Put the two signs at opposite ends of the room. Read out ordinary activities one at a time: praying, revising for a test, washing up, singing in church, playing football, listening to a friend.
Ask everyone to stand near the sign they think fits each activity, and ask a few people why.
Read Tozer’s line, “The motive is everything,” and ask how each activity could be done for God.
Ask everyone to choose privately their most boring task this week and to say before they start it, “This is for you.” Then invite them to look again at the sentence they wrote in week one.
